katakana-chart.intro_tr: Katakana (カタカナ) is one of the two Japanese phonetic syllabaries, covering the exact same 46 basic sounds as hiragana but written with more angular, straight-edged shapes. It is used mainly for loanwords (gairaigo) borrowed from other languages, foreign personal and place names, onomatopoeia, scientific/technical terms, and for stylistic emphasis (similar to italics in English). Because Japanese has a limited native sound inventory, katakana developed a set of extended combinations (like ファ, ティ, ヴァ) to approximate foreign sounds such as f, v, ti, and w-glides that don't exist in the native syllable set. Two marks are essentially exclusive to katakana usage: the long vowel bar ー (chōonpu) and the middle dot ・ (nakaguro) used to separate foreign name elements. Mastering this chart is a prerequisite for reading any menu, ad, brand name, or piece of modern Japanese text.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Katakana Chart — Gojūon (46 core sounds)
footnotes_tr: シ is pronounced 'shi', チ is 'chi', ツ is 'tsu', フ is 'fu' — these do not follow the plain consonant+vowel pattern.
ヲ is almost never used in katakana text; it survives mainly as a historical/stylistic curiosity (the hiragana を is the real object-marker particle).
ン never starts a word and has no vowel of its own — it represents a syllabic 'n' sound.

tables.caption_tr: Voiced (゛ dakuten) and Semi-voiced (゜ handakuten) Katakana
footnotes_tr: ヂ and ヅ are extremely rare in katakana loanwords; ジ and ズ are used instead in almost all cases.
The handakuten (゜) only ever attaches to the h-row (ハヒフヘホ → パピプペポ).

tables.caption_tr: Contracted Sounds — Yōon (small ャ/ュ/ョ combinations)
footnotes_tr: The small ャュョ are written at reduced size and never pronounced as a separate syllable — they fuse with the preceding consonant to form one mora.

tables.caption_tr: Extended Katakana for Foreign Sounds (used only in loanwords)
rows: トゥ (rare, e.g. in some transliterations)
footnotes_tr: These combinations were created after WWII specifically to write foreign sounds more accurately (e.g. 'v' via ヴ, since native Japanese has no 'v').
In casual writing ヴ is often replaced with the simpler ブ (e.g. バイオリン instead of ヴァイオリン).

tables.caption_tr: Special Marks Unique or Central to Katakana
rows: Lengthens the preceding vowel by one mora; hiragana instead repeats the vowel kana (e.g. おかあさん vs コーヒー)
コーヒー (kōhī, coffee), ケーキ (kēki, cake)
Doubles the following consonant, creating a brief stop
ベッド (beddo, bed), サッカー (sakkā, soccer)
Separates elements of foreign names or items in a list
テレビ (TV), パン (bread, from Portuguese)
By far the most common use of katakana
Japanese names normally use kanji or hiragana instead
ワンワン (bow-wow), ドキドキ (heart pounding)
Can also be written in hiragana; katakana adds punch/emphasis
Common in advertising, manga, and casual text
ソニー (Sony), トヨタ (Toyota, sometimes kanji)
Many Japanese brands choose katakana for a modern feel

examples.translation_tr: coffee — note the ー (chōonpu) lengthening the final vowel
soccer/football — note the small ッ doubling the 'k' sound
party — combines the extended sound ティ with the long vowel mark ー
check / to check — uses the extended combination チェ
violin — uses ヴァ to represent the 'va' sound not native to Japanese
John Smith — the ・ (nakaguro) separates a foreign first and last name
